title: Pentagon Pours $560M Into Australian Scandium Project; Houthis Hit Jazan Refinery After Makkah Pact; Vance Calls Modi on Energy and Minerals
subhead: The US Department of War commits US$400M to Sunrise Energy Metals' scandium mine in NSW — the largest Western critical minerals investment yet — while Houthi drone strikes on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery signal that the Makkah defence pact's deterrence is already being tested.

sections.heading: Pentagon Backs World-First Scandium Mine With US$400M Loan
sections.body:
The US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital has issued a conditional commitment for up to US$400 million (A$570 million) in 25-year debt financing for Sunrise Energy Metals' Syerston Scandium Project in New South Wales, Australia. The project targets initial production of 60 tonnes per annum of high-purity scandium oxide over an estimated 32-year mine life, with potential expansion to 180 tpa — positioning it as the cornerstone of Western scandium supply.

The loan comes days after President Trump hosted a critical minerals meeting at the State Department on Friday, where he announced US$3 billion in broader critical minerals investments and declared the US would reclaim its place as 'the minerals superpower of the world.' Executives from BHP and Rio Tinto also attended, according to The Australian Financial Review and Motley Fool Australia.

Sunrise chairman Robert Friedland called the financing 'a landmark moment' that aligns with the US-Australia Partnership on critical minerals. The company also announced plans for a US securities exchange listing and said the revised capital estimate for Syerston is A$450–475 million, with first production targeted for late 2028. Sunrise shares have risen more than 1,200% over the past 12 months.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the single largest Western government commitment to a scandium project — a mineral vital for aerospace alloys, solid oxide fuel cells, and defence applications where China currently dominates supply. The Pentagon's direct financing marks a shift from rhetoric to capital deployment in the critical minerals race.

sections.heading: Houthis Strike Jazan Refinery Two Days After Makkah Defence Pact
sections.body:
Houthi militants claimed a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Sunday, August 9, according to Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree. The 400,000 barrel-per-day refinery in south-western Saudi Arabia processes crude for domestic and export markets. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry confirmed a fire broke out at the facility but was later extinguished with no injuries reported.

The strike came two days after Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement — a collective-defence pact declaring that an armed attack on any signatory shall be regarded as an attack on all. The Houthis explicitly linked the attack to the pact, calling it a response to the kingdom's alignment with Sunni allies amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, according to ABC Australia.

Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar described the agreement as 'purely defensive in nature' and open to other nations, while Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said it was not aimed at Iran. However, as Firstpost analysis noted, Pakistan refrained from military action under its existing bilateral defence commitment to Saudi Arabia when Iran struck Saudi territory earlier this year — raising questions about the pact's credibility as a deterrent.
sections.whyItMatters: The Jazan strike is a direct test of the Makkah pact's deterrence value. The fact that Houthi forces struck Saudi infrastructure within 48 hours of a mutual defence agreement suggests the pact's signalling effect has limits against non-state actors already at war.

sections.heading: Vance Calls Modi as Senate Sanctions Bill Looms Over India
sections.body:
US Vice President JD Vance called Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday, August 8, to discuss expanding the India-US comprehensive global strategic partnership across trade, defence, energy security, and critical minerals, according to an Indian government readout. The call came one day after the US Senate voted 86-11 to approve the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which authorises the president to impose 100% tariffs on goods from the top five importers of Russian oil and gas — currently China, India, Azerbaijan, Hungary, and Slovakia.

India, which remains a major buyer of Russian crude, faces significant exposure. The Indian readout made no mention of the sanctions bill or the proposed trade deal, noting only that the two leaders 'exchanged views on regional and global developments of mutual interest.' The American side has not yet released its own summary of the conversation.

Relations between New Delhi and Washington have been strained by US tariffs on India and Trump's repeated claims of having resolved the India-Pakistan military clashes of May 2025 — claims India has firmly rejected, maintaining the ceasefire was bilateral. Both sides have recently made efforts to repair ties, with Modi and Trump directing officials in June to work toward a 'balanced, mutually beneficial' trade agreement.
sections.whyItMatters: The Vance-Modi call is the first high-level US-India engagement since the Senate sanctions bill. India's silence on the bill in the readout is telling — New Delhi must now balance its reliance on discounted Russian crude against the risk of 100% tariffs on its exports to the US.

sections.heading: Iran-Oman Hormuz Deal 'Final Stages' but Strait Stays Shut
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that an agreement with Oman to establish new shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz was in its 'final stages,' but stressed the deal alone would not result in reopening the waterway. Iran's conditions for reopening include US compensation for attacks, lifting of sanctions, an end to military threats, and withdrawal of US forces from the region.

Araqchi also said Iran and the US are not engaged in talks and Tehran will not start them as long as Washington breaches the June interim deal. Messages are being exchanged via intermediaries. Trump told Axios the US was 'only semi-negotiating' with Iran and was 'low-keying it,' adding: 'It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game.'

A US official told Reuters on Friday that Washington expects an Iran-Oman agreement soon and that the US could lift its blockade of Iranian ports once commercial vessels can transit the region without obstruction. But the gap between 'final stages' and actual reopening remains wide.
sections.whyItMatters: The pattern is now familiar: diplomatic signals of progress followed by Iranian insistence on conditions that Washington is unlikely to meet anytime soon. Each cycle of near-deal optimism and subsequent disappointment adds to oil's risk premium.

sections.heading: Oil Rises Toward $85 on Hormuz Uncertainty, Supply Attacks
sections.body:
Brent crude rose 91 cents (1.09%) to $84.46 a barrel and WTI climbed 61 cents (0.78%) to $78.79 in early Monday trading, Reuters reported, reversing some of last week's 7% decline that had been driven by premature optimism about a Hormuz reopening. Both benchmarks are now on their third rising session.

KCM Trade chief market analyst Tim Waterer said traders have been 'conditioned by the on-again, off-again nature of the negotiations' and are waiting for 'tangible evidence, such as verified tanker movements or formal agreements, before further unwinding the risk premium.' ADNOC separately reported that 15 of its vessels have been attacked transiting the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began, underscoring the ongoing physical risk to shipping.

US stock futures were largely flat on Sunday night, with the S&P 500 slipping 0.1% to 7,775.50. Investors are balancing geopolitical risk against weak July jobs data — the US economy lost 23,000 jobs last month versus expectations of an 80,000 gain — which has eased pressure for a Federal Reserve rate hike.
sections.whyItMatters: Oil's recovery reflects the market pricing in a slower Hormuz reopening than hoped. The combination of Iranian intransigence on conditions, Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, and continued shipping disruptions keeps the geopolitical risk premium firmly embedded.

sections.heading: Cyprus Gas to Reach Europe by Early 2028
sections.body:
Cyprus Energy Minister Michael Damianos told the Associated Press that natural gas from the Cronos field off Cyprus's southern coast will reach European markets as early as March 2028, after TotalEnergies and Eni made a final investment decision last month. Gas will flow through a 105-kilometre pipeline to Egypt's Zohr field, then to the Damietta LNG facility for liquefaction and shipment to Europe — a project estimated at roughly US$2 billion, about half the cost of developing other Cypriot fields due to proximity to existing infrastructure.

Cronos holds over 3 trillion cubic feet of gas, with a provision allowing up to 20% to cover Egyptian domestic needs. Damianos stressed the project's significance is not revenue — 'its importance is the commencement of being a producer and having first gas' — but rather establishing Cyprus as a new supplier to a continent urgently diversifying away from Russian gas.

ExxonMobil and QatarEnergy expect gas from the larger Glaucus and Pegasus fields (combined 6.9 tcf) by 2033. A Chevron-led venture is targeting a final decision on the 5.6 tcf Aphrodite field by summer 2027.
sections.whyItMatters: Cyprus's Cronos-to-Europe pipeline is the first concrete EastMed supply route to reach final investment decision, offering the EU a new non-Russian, non-Middle-East gas source by 2028. It's modest in scale but symbolically important for European energy diversification.

bottomLine: The Pentagon's US$400M commitment to an Australian scandium project marks the most significant Western capital deployment in the critical minerals race to date, turning Trump's minerals-superpower rhetoric into real financing. Meanwhile, the Houthi strike on Jazan — within 48 hours of the Makkah defence pact — exposes the limits of state-level security agreements against non-state actors already at war. Oil is drifting back toward $85 as Hormuz reopening optimism fades against Iran's non-negotiable conditions and continued attacks on Gulf infrastructure. India faces a growing strategic bind: Vance's call signals engagement, but the Senate's 100% tariff threat on Russian oil buyers looms directly over New Delhi.
sources: Reuters, ABC Australia, Motley Fool Australia, The Australian Financial Review, Firstpost, The Hindu, AP via CSMonitor, EconoTimes, Global Banking & Finance Review, Rediff, CNBCTV18, Seeking Alpha, Tradewinds
